lead: Guidance is the part of avionics that turns 'where the target is' into 'how hard to turn'. This unit covers the guidance laws of missiles — command, homing, pursuit, CLOS and proportional navigation — plus the airframe, fin servos and roll and lateral autopilots that carry the commands out, ending with spacecraft power, thermal and attitude control. After it you can classify any guidance scheme, compute a proportional navigation acceleration command, size a fin servo, and explain how a satellite is powered and pointed.
about: The unit follows a missile from the first steering command to the fin that flies it, then lifts the same ideas into space. Chapter 6.1 shows the flight management system, the civil box that plans a route and hands guidance to the autopilot. Chapter 6.2 sorts guidance laws into four families. Chapter 6.3 opens the command and homing families, and 6.4 explains pursuit, line-of-sight and CLOS, the laws that aim at the target or hold a line. Chapter 6.5 turns the line-of-sight rate into the proportional navigation command and its variants. Chapters 6.6 and 6.7 carry the command into hardware: airframe, fin actuation servos, roll and lateral autopilots, and bank-to-turn flight. Chapter 6.8 closes with spacecraft power, thermal and attitude control, where there is no pilot to help.

chapters.idea: The flight management system is the on-board computer that holds the flight plan, predicts time and fuel, and sends steering commands to the autopilot.
chapters.depth: Treat the FMS as one line replaceable unit with four jobs: navigation (blending GPS, INS and radio positions), flight planning (route, waypoints, legs), performance (speed, altitude, fuel and time predictions) and guidance (LNAV and VNAV commands to the autopilot and flight director). Cover the two databases: the navigation database of waypoints and airways, and the performance database of aircraft speeds and fuel flows. Cover the MCDU and the pages a crew uses, and the alert messages for an invalid route. Only a few universities teach this inside a guidance unit; it usually sits in flight control syllabi, so keep it at block level.

figure.title: Flight management system
figure.aria: Block diagram: navigation sensors and two databases feed the FMS core, which sends LNAV and VNAV guidance to the autopilot.

chapters.example: An aircraft flies 900 NM at a true airspeed of 450 kt into a 50 kt headwind. Its fuel flow is 2400 kg/h. Find the ground speed, the time and the fuel burn. Ground speed = 450 − 50 = 400 kt. Time = 900 ÷ 400 = 2.25 h = 2 h 15 min. Fuel = 2400 × 2.25 = 5400 kg. These are the numbers the performance page shows before departure.
chapters.trap: Mixing up the FMS with the autopilot. The FMS computes the steering command; the autopilot and flight director fly it. Also keep the two databases apart: the navigation database holds places, the performance database holds aircraft numbers.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1, autopilot and automatic flight control.
chapters.leave: Fly-by-wire, servo tabs and Q-feel to Unit 1; LRU and IMA packaging to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Every guidance law is a rule for turning target information into an acceleration command, and the laws fall into four families.
chapters.depth: Start with the guidance loop: a sensor or seeker measures the target, the guidance law computes a commanded acceleration, and the autopilot and fins produce it. Then build the taxonomy. Command guidance: MCLOS, SACLOS and beam riding. Homing guidance: active, semi-active and passive. Navigation guidance: pursuit, line of sight, CLOS and proportional navigation. Modern guidance: optimal, differential-game, sliding-mode and estimation-based laws. Some syllabi call pursuit, LOS, CLOS and PN the classical guidance laws and put everything else under modern. Give one line per family, with no mathematics here; the maths comes in Chapters 6.4 and 6.5.

figure.aria: Tree of guidance laws branching into command, homing, navigation and modern families, each with its common members.

chapters.example: A missile closes on a target at 800 m/s and is 4 km away. It must remove a 200 m sideways error. Find the time to go and the average lateral acceleration needed. Time t = 4000 ÷ 800 = 5 s. Using y = ½ a t², a = 2y ÷ t² = 2 × 200 ÷ 25 = 16 m/s² = 1.63 g. Whichever family of laws produces this command, the number is the same.
chapters.trap: Treating the families as alternatives at one level. Command and homing say where the guidance computer sits; pursuit, CLOS and PN say what rule it runs. A homing missile can use a PN rule.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for the autopilot that receives the command.
chapters.leave: Seeker and radar hardware to Unit 5; the fin loop to Chapters 6.6 and 6.7.

chapters.idea: In command guidance the guidance computer stays on the ground or launcher; in homing guidance the computer travels inside the missile.
chapters.depth: Command guidance: a launcher radar or an operator tracks target and missile, a computer works out the correction, and a radio or wire link sends it. Cover MCLOS, where the operator steers the missile by joystick; SACLOS, where the operator only keeps the sight on the target and the computer flies the missile; and beam riding, where the missile stays inside a radar or laser beam. Homing guidance: a seeker in the nose. Active means the missile carries transmitter and receiver. Semi-active means the launcher illuminates and the missile only receives the reflection. Passive means the missile listens to radiation the target emits. Compare range, accuracy, cost and countermeasures in a short list.

figure.title: Command guidance loop
figure.aria: Flowchart: the tracker observes the target, the computer forms a command, the uplink sends it to the missile, and the missile position returns to the tracker.

chapters.example: A SACLOS system sees the missile 3 mrad off the line of sight at 2 km range. Closing speed is 800 m/s. Find the offset and the acceleration the computer must command. Offset = 2000 × 0.003 = 6 m. Time to go t = 2000 ÷ 800 = 2.5 s. a = 2y ÷ t² = 2 × 6 ÷ 6.25 = 1.92 m/s², about 0.2 g.
chapters.trap: Calling semi-active passive. A semi-active missile carries a receiver and no transmitter, but the target is still lit up by the launcher; a passive missile uses radiation the target itself gives off.
chapters.leave: Seeker optics, detectors and radar signal processing to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Pursuit aims the missile at the target, CLOS holds the missile on the line from launcher to target, and neither zeroes the line-of-sight rate that a hit really needs.
chapters.depth: Define the line of sight (LOS) as the straight line from missile to target, and the LOS rate λ̇ as the speed at which its direction turns. Pure pursuit points the velocity vector at the target: always a tail chase, the LOS rate never reaches zero, and the lateral demand peaks near the end. Deviated pursuit uses a fixed lead angle. The collision or constant-bearing course holds the LOS direction fixed, which is the true intercept condition. CLOS keeps the missile on the launcher-to-target line; beam riding is its radar version. Give the lead angle relation sin θ = (Vt ÷ Vm) sin β with θ the lead angle, Vt and Vm the target and missile speeds, and β the angle between the target velocity and the LOS. Add the qualitative picture: a curved path from the rear, a nearly straight path from the front.

figure.aria: Engagement geometry: the missile and the target each run to a common collision point, with the line of sight drawn between them.

chapters.example: A missile flies at 600 m/s. The target flies at 300 m/s and its velocity makes 60° with the line of sight. Find the lead angle for a collision course. sin θ = (Vt ÷ Vm) sin β = (300 ÷ 600) × sin 60° = 0.5 × 0.866 = 0.433. θ = 25.7°. Pure pursuit uses θ = 0 and needs no such sum, but it curves the path and demands large lateral acceleration at the end.
chapters.trap: Calling pure pursuit a collision course. Only a constant-bearing course has zero LOS rate; in pure pursuit the LOS keeps turning all the way in.
chapters.leave: The law that drives LOS rate to zero is Chapter 6.5.

chapters.idea: Proportional navigation commands acceleration proportional to the line-of-sight rate, the cheapest way to force the missile onto a collision course.
chapters.depth: Base form a = N Vc λ̇, where N is the effective navigation ratio (usually 3 to 5, dimensionless), Vc is the closing velocity in m/s and λ̇ is the LOS rate in rad/s. Explain why zero LOS rate means intercept and why an acceleration proportional to λ̇ drives it to zero. Then the variants. Pure PN (PPN): acceleration perpendicular to the LOS, using Vc. True PN (TPN): acceleration perpendicular to the missile velocity, using Vm. Augmented PN (APN): adds (N ÷ 2) times the target acceleration normal to the LOS. Biased PN (BPN): adds a bias term. Generalised PN (GPN): a general form that reduces to APN. Ideal PN (IPN): the exact geometry form kept without small-angle approximations, used to check what PPN loses. Qualitative analysis: PPN against a non-manoeuvring target gives near-zero miss distance with bounded acceleration; against a manoeuvring target PPN leaves a steady-state miss unless N is large, while APN cancels the target manoeuvre. Higher N lowers miss distance but raises acceleration demand and noise sensitivity.

figure.aria: Plot of commanded acceleration against line-of-sight rate for navigation ratios 3, 4 and 5 at a closing speed of 900 m/s; the middle line passes through 72 m/s² at 0.02 rad/s.

chapters.example: A missile closes at Vc = 900 m/s with its own speed Vm = 600 m/s. The seeker measures a LOS rate of 0.02 rad/s. Take N = 4 and g = 9.81 m/s². PPN: a = N Vc λ̇ = 4 × 900 × 0.02 = 72 m/s² = 7.3 g, perpendicular to the LOS. TPN: a = N Vm λ̇ = 4 × 600 × 0.02 = 48 m/s² = 4.9 g, perpendicular to the missile velocity.
chapters.trap: Putting Vm into the PPN formula or Vc into the TPN formula, and feeding λ̇ in degrees per second. The law needs rad/s, and N carries no units.
chapters.leave: Producing this acceleration is Chapters 6.6 and 6.7.

chapters.idea: The airframe, the fin servos and the choice of control type decide how fast and how accurately a guidance command becomes a real turn.
chapters.depth: Airframe: nose seeker dome, body, and either canard fins near the nose or tail fins, with lift coming from body angle of attack and from the fins. Propulsion in one short survey only: solid rocket motor for short range, ramjet for long-range cruise, thrust vector control during boost when fin authority is low. Control types: aerodynamic fin control, reaction jets or thrust vector control outside the atmosphere, and the skid-to-turn against bank-to-turn choice. Fin actuation servos: electric, electro-hydraulic or pneumatic; the chain command, amplifier, torque motor and servo valve, ram, fin, with position feedback; torque limit, rate limit and hinge moment. Gyroscope types used in missiles (rate gyro, free gyro, dynamically tuned gyro) are named here, but their physics is in Unit 5. Only a few universities teach this depth.

figure.title: Fin actuation chain
figure.aria: Chain from the acceleration command through amplifier, servo valve and ram to the fin, with fin position fed back to the amplifier.

chapters.example: A fin needs 30 N·m of hinge torque and must slew 2° in 20 ms. The push rod acts 25 mm from the hinge. Find the rod force, the slew rate and the actuator power. Force = 30 ÷ 0.025 = 1200 N. Slew rate = 2° ÷ 0.02 s = 100 °/s = 1.745 rad/s. Power = torque × rate = 30 × 1.745 = 52.4 W.
chapters.trap: Confusing hinge moment with actuator torque and dropping the lever arm. A servo can also be torque-limited or rate-limited, and the two give very different step responses.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 hydraulic and pneumatic supply; Unit 3 actuators; Chapter 6.5 for the command.
chapters.leave: Hydraulic and pneumatic circuits to Unit 2; gyro physics to Unit 5; the closed loops to Chapter 6.7.

chapters.idea: The roll autopilot holds the missile steady about its long axis, the lateral autopilot converts a yaw command into acceleration, and bank-to-turn rolls the whole airframe so its lift does the turning.
chapters.depth: Roll autopilot: a gyro measures roll angle or roll rate, and a proportional plus rate loop drives ailerons or roll fins to hold attitude or wings level. Lateral autopilot: outer loop on lateral acceleration, inner loop on yaw rate, gains scheduled with Mach and altitude, with the accelerometer and rate gyro of Unit 4 as sensors. Gyroscope types in the loop: rate gyro for damping, free or vertical gyro for attitude, and dynamically tuned, ring laser or fibre optic gyros in modern missiles. Then bank-to-turn: the missile rolls until its single lift plane points along the commanded acceleration, then pulls. Commanded bank angle satisfies sin φ = a_side ÷ a_total. Compare with skid-to-turn: BTT uses one lifting surface, gives less drag and longer range, but needs a high roll rate, suffers inertia cross-coupling and reverses direction slowly.

figure.title: Roll autopilot loop
figure.aria: Roll loop: the roll command enters the autopilot, the fins roll the missile, and a rate gyro feeds roll rate back to the autopilot.

chapters.example: A bank-to-turn missile must accelerate at 8 g in a direction that lies 4 g to the side of its lift plane. Find the bank angle and the lift the wing must give. sin φ = 4 ÷ 8 = 0.5, so φ = 30°. Lift in the body plane = 8 × cos 30° = 6.93 g. The roll autopilot must settle at 30° before the lateral autopilot pulls 6.93 g.
chapters.trap: Saying the roll itself turns a BTT missile. Roll only points the lift vector; the turn comes from the angle of attack applied after the roll. Also, roll loop bandwidth must sit well above the lateral loop.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.6 for the airframe and servos; Unit 1 for autopilot basics.
chapters.leave: Gyro construction and precession to Unit 5; fly-by-wire and active control to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: A spacecraft must make, store and dump energy, hold its temperature inside limits, and point its payload, all without a pilot.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this inside an avionics unit; keep it at system-block level. Power: solar array, battery, power conditioning and distribution unit, shunt or maximum-power-point regulation, and the eclipse energy balance. Thermal: multi-layer insulation, radiators sized by Q = ε σ A T⁴ with Q the heat dumped in W, ε the emissivity, σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/(m²·K⁴) and T the absolute temperature in K, heaters, heat pipes, passive against active control. Attitude control: spin stabilisation and three-axis control by reaction wheels, momentum wheels, control moment gyros, thrusters and magnetorquers; sensors are the sun sensor, star tracker, earth sensor and gyro; disturbance torques come from gravity gradient, solar radiation pressure and residual atmosphere; the control law is proportional-derivative and wheels need desaturation.

figure.aria: Layer list of spacecraft bus subsystems from payload down to structure, each with a short note on what it carries.

chapters.example: A 500 W payload flies in a 96 min orbit with a 35 min eclipse. The battery may use 90% depth of discharge at 90% discharge efficiency. The array works for the other 61 min and 10% of its output is lost. Find the battery capacity and the array size. Eclipse energy = 500 × (35 ÷ 60) = 291.7 Wh. Capacity = 291.7 ÷ (0.9 × 0.9) = 360 Wh. Recharge power = 291.7 ÷ (61 ÷ 60) = 287 W. Array output = 500 + 287 = 787 W; with losses, 787 ÷ 0.9 = 875 W.
chapters.trap: Sizing the array for the payload alone and forgetting the recharge energy, or using the full orbit period instead of the eclipse time when sizing the battery.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 for power generation and batteries; Unit 4 for spacecraft avionics.
chapters.leave: Battery chemistry to Unit 3; attitude sensors and Kalman filtering to Unit 5; avionics architecture to Unit 4.
